analysis.one_liner: Exempts estates and gifts up to $5 million from federal estate tax, with the exemption rising with inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee, drew zero cosponsors, and died when the Congress ended in January 2003 without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal estate and gift tax exemption to $5 million per person, up from the $675,000 in effect in 2001, and increased it each year with inflation. Only the estates of people leaving more than that would pay any tax. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates. A $5 million exemption, adjusted for inflation, would spare virtually every estate in the country from federal estate tax, with the largest savings going to families inheriting millions of dollars.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the unified credit against estate and gift taxes so that the first $5 million of an estate or lifetime gifts is tax-free.
Adjusts the $5 million amount upward each year after 2001 by a cost-of-living formula, rounded to the nearest $10,000.
The change would apply to deaths and gifts occurring after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The estate tax is paid almost entirely by estates above the exemption, so raising the exemption to $5 million cuts federal revenue that otherwise comes from the largest inheritances, leaving other taxes higher, services lower, or deficits larger than they would otherwise be.

drawbacks.text: The benefit is concentrated at the very top: only estates exceeding the exemption owe any estate tax, so a $5 million exemption would eliminate the tax for nearly all estates while cutting revenue the government collects from the largest inheritances.
The inflation adjustment would make the revenue loss grow automatically each year, since fewer estates would cross the rising threshold over time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's entire benefit goes to families inheriting the largest estates, while the cost — lost federal revenue — is spread across everyone who pays federal taxes. A fair-minded case exists for protecting heirs of family farms and small businesses from forced sales, but a $5 million exemption goes far beyond that, shielding multi-million-dollar inheritances entirely. This context mattered: the 2001 Congress was already phasing out the estate tax under a separate law, making this standalone bill largely redundant.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Deutsch introduced the bill on April 4, 2001, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
No cosponsors signed on — the cosponsor list shows zero.
The action history records no committee vote, no markup, no floor action, and no vote in either chamber; the bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal treasury — and the taxpayers who fund it — kept estate tax revenue from the largest estates, since the exemption was never raised. Heirs of multimillion-dollar estates lost the chance at a tax break they would have gained if it had passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers, who kept estate tax revenue

for.name: Rep. Peter Deutsch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter in Congress; no member cosponsored it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never held a markup or vote on it; it never left the committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only record of support is a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Heirs and families of the wealthiest households
industries.note: The bill would have spared estates up to $5 million (rising with inflation) from federal estate tax, a benefit worth millions to the largest inheritances. Because the bill never advanced, these families gained nothing and the estate tax continued to apply above much lower thresholds.

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys and wealth advisors
industries.note: A much higher exemption would have shrunk the need for estate-tax planning services, since far fewer estates would owe the tax. The bill's failure preserved demand for those services.
